chunks: And what Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Ibn Faddal from Hammad from Al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): regarding the sale of the nursing mother.

He said, 'There is no harm in that if there is need.' These two narrations do not contradict the narrations we presented earlier, because they are more numerous and more mutually consistent, so it is not permissible to abandon those and act upon these. Moreover, the matter is as we described, on the assumption that the way to reconcile them is if the nursing has not reached the limit that causes prohibition, for in that case, her sale is permissible in all circumstances. As for the first narration, it is possible that what is meant by 'except' is not exception, but rather 'except' was used to mean 'and', which is known in language, as if he said: 'If a man owns his father, he is free, and whatever is due to nursing.'

As for the latter narration, it is possible that the sale of the nursing mother was permissible for the father of the boy, according to what we presented earlier in the narration of Isḥāq ibn ʿAmmār from the Impartial One (peace be upon him), and it is not meant that this is permissible for the nursling. There is no explicit statement in the narration to that effect, but it is compatible with what we said, and if so, it does not contradict what we presented earlier.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a slave woman who is a nursing mother in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi employs the principle of *jam'* (reconciliation) to harmonize narrations regarding the sale of an *umm al-walad* (mother of the child) by distinguishing between the permanence of the nursing bond (*radāʿ*) and the necessity (*ḥājah*) for sale. He further refines the ruling by analyzing linguistic ambiguities, suggesting the permission may apply specifically to the father’s ownership rights rather than the nursling’s, thereby preserving the consistency of the broader juristic corpus.
